stem: A72-year-old woman is referred to the Haematology Unit after suffering prolonged epistaxis. She takes regular methotrexate to control her rheumatoid arthritis. Physical examination reveals small joint arthritis and synovitis bilaterally but there are no other findings. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 102 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 4.9×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 163×10/L 150-400×10/L Prothrombin time(PT) 13 seconds 12-14.8 seconds Activated partial thromboplastin time 72 seconds (APTT) Does not correct on mixing with normal 27-41 seconds plasma Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Acquired Haemophilia A is seen in patients with autoimmune disease including rheumatoid arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus and in haematological malignancies. It is caused by a factor VIll inhibiting antibody which prevents its activity. This is why the clotting abnormality fails to correct with normal plasma mixing. The condition is difficult to treat, options can include therapies to increase factor VIll and to use bypassing agents such as recombinant factor VII. Haemophilia Media explanations.

stem: A 27-year-old man is referred to the Cardiology Clinic by his General Practitioner because of a heart murmur. He is tall and thin with a long arm span and has suffered from recurrent shoulder dislocation. His blood pressure is 135/65 mmHg. His heart rate is 69 bpm and regular. There is an early diastolic murmur heard best to the left of the sternum in the third intercostal space. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the murmur?
explanation: Aortic regurgitation is best heard in the third left intercostal space and is an early diastolic murmur. It is more commonly seen in patients with Marfan syndrome which is suggested by this patient's long arm span and recurrent shoulder dislocation. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging is recommended in patients with Marfan syndrome to allow detailed characterisation of the aortic root. Combined aortic root and valve replacement may be required. Q.

stem: A 49-year-old man is referred to the Rheumatology Clinic with arthritis predominantly affecting his hands and feet. He is finding it difficult to continue his job as a computer operator because of pain. There is nail pitting and he has evidence of distal interphalangeal joint arthritis.X-ray of the hands shows erosion of the distal tuft of the distal phalanges of the fingers. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The pattern of this patient's arthritis, affecting the distal interphalangeal joints with nail pitting and distal bony erosion on the hand x-ray fits well with a diagnosis of psoriatic arthritis. Although most patients develop skin psoriasis before arthritis, 20% of patients with arthritis develop joint disease only. Autoantibodies do not have a role in confirming the diagnosis,although inflammatory markers may be elevated. Methotrexate and anti-tumour necrosis factor biologicals are the mainstay of therapy. Q.

stem: A35-year-old man presents to the Rheumatology Clinic complaining that both of his hands turn white if he goes out on a cold morning or puts his hands into cold water. He works as a tree surgeon and is often out in the cold. He smokes 15 cigarettes per day and drinks 10 units of alcohol per week. He also experiences intense pain in the fingers, which later turn blue and eventually red, with a sensation of warmth. He has lost fine touch and temperature discrimination on examination of both hands. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This patient has an occupation where they are likely to have used vibrating power tools such as a chainsaw on a regular basis. It leads to loss of fine touch sensation and proprioception as well as symptoms of secondary Raynaud's phenomenon. If possible, the source of the vibration should be removed. Drugs such as nifedipine or amlodipine may be useful in driving peripheral vasodilatation to relieve symptoms of Raynaud's phenomenon. Q.

stem: A72-year-old smoker is reviewed in the Oncology Clinic following a bronchoscopy and biopsy of a lung lesion that has confirmed a squamous cell carcinoma of the bronchus. What electrolyte abnormality is most likely to be found on investigation?
explanation: An incidence of up to 23% of hypercalcaemia has been reported in patients with squamous cell carcinoma of the bronchus. It occurs because of parathyroid hormone-related peptide production which leads to hypercalcaemia and hypophosphataemia. Initial treatment of hypercalcaemia when it presents acutely is with normal saline rehydration and bisphosphonate therapy. Treatment of the underlying tumour reduces calcium levels. Parathyroid hormone-related peptide is also occasionally secreted by breast cancers. Q.

stem: A71-year-old man who has a chronic venous leg ulcer over the left medial malleolus is referred to the Dermatology Clinic for a new enlarging nodule at the margin of the ulcer. Examination reveals a 1cm nodular ulcerated lesion with a necrotic centre. It is adjacent to slough and erythema related to the venous ulcer. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the nodule?
explanation: Patients with chronic venous ulcers are at significant risk of squamous cell carcinomas forming at the margin. That is the most likely explanation for the new ulcerated nodule which has formed here. Excision of the lesion as early as possible is the intervention of choice, although given chronic venous insufficiency, achieving healing with long term skin closure may be difficult. Difficuty:Average.

stem: A72-year-old woman who has end-stage chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and is on triple inhaled therapy and home oxygen, presents to the Emergency Department with sudden-onset left-sided pleuritic chest pain. She has decreased breath sounds on auscultation of the left lung and has a 2.5 cm rim of air on her chest X-ray. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Air aspiration followed by chest drain if it fails
High flow oxygen and observe for 24 hours
explanation: This patient has a secondary pneumothorax which has a rim of air measuring greater than 2 cm. As such formal chest drain insertion is the only possible option. Aspiration can only be considered in the treatment of secondary pneumothorax where the size is between 1cm and 2 cm.The patient should then be admitted for high-flow oxygen and if air aspiration fails, a chest drain should be inserted. Q.

stem: A72-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with sudden-onset, severe vertigo, with nausea and vomiting. He also has dysphonia, dysarthria, dysphagia and left Horner syndrome. He is ataxic and falls towards the left-hand side when he tries to walk. There is pain and numbness affecting the left side of the face. He has minimal weakness on the right-hand side of the body,with impaired pain and temperature sensation affecting the right arm and the right leg. Which artery is most likely to have been occluded?
explanation: This patient's symptoms are typical of those seen in lateral medullary syndrome where a stroke affecting the lateral medulla occurs due to occlusion of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery or the vertebral artery. Outcomes in lateral medullary syndrome depend on the size of the lesion, although more than 85% of patients recover with minimal symptoms at six months. Anticoagulation is initiated where there is atrial fibrillation and antiplatelet therapy is considered in other patients who have suffered an infarct. Q.

stem: A35-year-old man is referred to the Renal Clinic for assessment of his hypertension. He is an amateur runner and exercises every day. His blood pressure is 155/90 mmHg and his body mass index is 22 kg/m. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 139 g/l 135-175 g/L White cell count(WCC) 6.4×109/L 4-11×10/L Platelets (PLT) 291×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 3.2 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Bicarbonate (HCO) 34 mmol/L 22-30 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 85μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Primary hyperaldosteronism is the most likely diagnosis here given the hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis and hypertension in the presence of normal renal function and normal body weight. The onset of hypertension in adulthood suggests the cause is primary hyperaldosteronism rather than Liddle syndrome. Measurement of renin and aldosterone levels and abdominal computed tomography scan is the initial investigation of choice. Dietary sodium restriction and mineralocorticoid antagonists are the initial interventions of choice, with surgery as the preferred curative option for a unilateral adrenal adenoma. Hyperaldosteronism explanations.

stem: A 29-year-old man presents to the Psychiatry Clinic complaining that he is worried about returning to work at a local bar.He has been off work for three months after an assault. He could not remember anything for the first four weeks after the assault but can describe the event accurately. He is now feeling depressed and wakes up at 04.45 am each morning. Apart from worrying about work, he is leading a normal life. Physical examination is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This patient has a short-term, stress-related, non-psychotic disturbance that has occurred as a result of his assault. More severe features, including replaying the event, which might be suggestive of post-traumatic stress disorder are absent here. Features consistent with depression, such as early morning wakening and excessive worry,fit with the diagnosis. A combination approach with psychotherapy and antidepressants is usually considered. Dificulty:Average.

stem: A 62-year-old man attends the Gastroenterology Clinic for review six weeks after eradication therapy for Helicobacter pylori. An upper gastrointestinal endoscopy conducted eight weeks ago showed multiple gastric erosions. He wants to be sure that his H.pyloriinfection has been eradicated. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: Urea breath testing was formerly the only non-invasive way to confirm a diagnosis of H.pylori infection. In accordance with NICE guidelines, re-testing for H.pylori is performed by a carbon 13 urea breath test. In the event that a false negative is suspected, eg where symptoms of dyspepsia return, then a breath test could be considered with endoscopy as well as a biopsy to follow if required. Dificulty:Average.

stem: A 28-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department by his parents. He has an unkempt appearance. According to his parents, he has thought for some weeks that the secret service is listening to his thoughts and tracking everything that he says. A few days ago, he became profoundly depressed and refused to wash or change his clothes. This has happened on two or three other occasions over the past six months. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The presence of paranoid delusions that the secret service is listening to his thoughts suggests a strong schizophreniform component to this patient's disease, and the intermittent periods of depression suggest that he is suffering from schizoaffective disorder. Other causes of psychiatric illness, including drug abuse, medication and organic illness, should be excluded before the diagnosis is made. Patients may have a primarily depressive, primarily manic or a mixed picture of mood disturbance. Treatment is with a combination of both atypical antipsychotics and psychological therapies. Dificulty:Average.

stem: A 29-year-old motorcyclist presents to the Musculoskeletal Clinic for review with left-sided neck and back pain after a motor vehicle accident. Weakness and wasting of the pectoralis and forearm flexor muscles of the left arm with reduced reflexes are noted. The right arm has normal tone, power and reflexes. Which of the following is most likely to have been injured?
options: Lateral cord of the brachial plexus
Medial cord of the brachial plexus
Posterior cord of the brachial plexus
Upper trunk of the brachial plexus
explanation: The medial cord of the brachial plexus originates from the C8 and T1 nerve roots and supplies a number of important nerves including the medial pectoral nerve and the medial root of the median nerve. These supply the pectoralis major and minor and all of the forearm flexors apart from the flexor carpi ulnaris and a portion of the flexor digitorum profundus. Difficuty:Average.

stem: A72-year-old man has suffered a stroke and has failed his swallow assessment. Initial attempts at placing a nasogastric tube are unsuccessful and he is awaiting X-ray-guided placement. Initial urea and electrolytes are in the normal range. Which of the following is the most appropriate with respect to this patient's intravenous fluid replacement?
options: 25g of glucose in total per day
explanation: 25ml of water per kg/day is the maintenance fluid requirement in elderly patients as recommended. In younger patients, a rate of 30 ml/kg/day may be considered. Higher levels of fluid replacement are needed in patients with greater losses, eg due to pyrexia or gastrointestinal disease. Difficuty:Average.

stem: A 29-year-old woman presents to the Renal Clinic after finding out she is 12 weeks pregnant. She had a renal transplant nine months ago for end-stage kidney disease as a result of Immunoglobulin A nephropathy. She also has epilepsy. Her medication includes antihypertensives and a tacrolimus-based immunosuppressive regimen. Which of her medications is contraindicated in pregnancy?
explanation: Exposure to treatment with an angiotensin-converting enzyme(ACE) inhibitor, such as lisinopril, during the second and third trimesters is known to induce human fetotoxicity. Toxic effects may include decreased renal function, oligohydramnios and delayed skull ossification. Toxicity in the neonatal period includes renal failure, hypotension and hyperkalaemia. Toxicity in the first trimester also cannot be excluded. Where possible, ACE inhibitors should be stopped before women get pregnant. Dificulty:Average.

stem: A 49-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a 48 hour history of shortness of breath, fever and cough productive of rusty coloured sputum. Her temperature is 38.9°℃ and her blood pressure is 100/70 mmHg. There are coarse crackles and decreased breath sounds at the right lung base on auscultation. She has a cold sore at the left-hand corner of her mouth. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's chest symptoms?
explanation: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a common cause of community-acquired pneumonia and fits with the right- sided consolidation and rusty coloured sputum seen here. Streptococcal pneumonia is particularly associated with the reactivation of the herpes simplex virus, which accounts for the cold sore seen here. Awareness of herpes reactivation is important because in ventilated patients colonisation of the respiratory tract by herpes simplex can occur. Dificulty:Average.

stem: A 22-year-old woman is referred to the Renal Clinic with microscopic haematuria and progressive high-tone hearing loss noted over the last 12 months. Her two brothers have end-stage renal disease and commenced dialysis in their late 20s. Her blood pressure is 132/85 mmHg, her heart rate is 75 bpm and regular. Her body mass index is 22 kg/m. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 122 g/L 115-155 g/l White cell count 7.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 185×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 140 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 132μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Alport syndrome is most often associated with an X-Linked dominant inheritance pattern. It occurs because of a defect in type IV collagen which leads to progressive renal failure and hearing loss. A gradual deterioration in vision is also seen. End-stage renal failure occurs between the ages of 16 and 37.The disease progresses much more rapidly in men than women. Control of blood pressure and proteinuria with angiotensin- converting enzyme inhibitors is a key component of therapy. Alport Syndrome explanations.
