stem: A 62-year-old man presents to the Ophthalmology Department for an assessment of his visual fields. He suffered a stroke three months earlier and would like to resume driving. Visual field assessment reveals a right superior homonymous quadrantanopia. Where is the most likely site of this patient's neurological lesion?
explanation: Temporal lobe lesions can lead to damage to the optic radiation which causes a superior homonymous quadrantanopia.This occurs on the opposite side to the lesion, so that a lefttemporal lobe lesion could produce the right superior homonymous quadrantanopia seen here.

stem: A74-year-old man is reviewed in the Medical Admissions Ward 12 hours after admission following the latest of a series of suspected epileptic seizures. He has ischaemic heart disease and first-degree heart block is noted. Which of the following anti-epileptics carries the least risk of heart block?
explanation: Primidone is metabolised to two barbiturate derivatives, phenobarbital and phenylethylmalonamide. It differs from many other anti-epileptics in not having an effect on sodium channels, which means it does not lead to bradycardia.

stem: A 65-year-old man presents to the Ophthalmology Clinic complaining of a blue discouration of his vision. He has type Il diabetes, ischaemic heart disease and erectile dysfunction. Which of the following medications he takes is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
explanation: Sildenafil is a selective phosphodiesterase type 5(PDE5) inhibitor used in the treatment of erectile dysfunction. At high doses, it has some PDE6 inhibitory activity. Phosphodiesterase 6(PDE6) is found exclusively in rod and cone photoreceptors. Inhibition of PDE6 is, therefore, recognised to lead to blue discolouration of vision. This is not normally seen when low-dose sildenafil is used. Studies have shown there is no effective long-term improvement in either colour vision or visual acuity.

stem: A 43-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with rapid-onset, painless loss of vision affecting her left eye. She has polymyalgia rheumatica, for which her General Practitioner prescribed a regular daily dose of 7.5mg of prednisolone. Fundoscopy reveals widespread flame-shaped haemorrhages affecting the left retina. Her body mass index is 31kg/m. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Widespread flame-shaped haemorrhages, coupled with rapid-onset, painless loss of vision, are consistent with a diagnosis of retinal vein occlusion. Most patients develop central retinal vein occlusion affecting one eye. Risk factors for central retinal vein occlusion include hypertension, diabetes mellitus and thrombophilic disorders. Most patients with central retinal vein occlusion develop some permanent visual loss and are at increased risk of complications, including macular oedema.

stem: A 34-year-old woman who follows a vegan diet presents to the Endocrine Clinic complaining of pain affecting the proximal portion of both lower limbs and proximal myopathy. Her corrected calcium is at the lower end of the normal range,(2.1 mmol/L). Which of the following is most likely to be found on further testing?
explanation: This patient's presentation is consistent with osteomalacia due to reduced dietary calcium and, probably also, reduced vitamin D intake, which is seen with increasing frequency in patients who follow a vegan diet. Low levels of calcium stimulate an increase in parathyroid hormone levels, which in turn, drives increased renal hydroxylation of vitamin D.A reduction in parathyroid hormone levels is seen once adequate calcium and vitamin D replacement is instigated. The serum phosphate is reduced in dietary calcium and vitamin D deficiency.

stem: A 45-year-old man, who has type I diabetes, is 30 minutes into his dialysis session on the Outpatient Renal Unit. He has started complaining of chills and light headedness and has developed a fever and an erythematous rash. His temperature is 38.1°℃, blood pressure is 95/60 mmHg and his heart rate is 105 bpm and regular. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
explanation: Given this patient is pyrexial and hypotensive the most likely cause of his symptoms is bacterial contamination of the giving set or the dialysis machine itself leading to production of endotoxin, which has driven a systemic inflammatory reaction. As soon as the diagnosis is suspected the patient should be removed from dialysis and samples taken for bacteriology.

stem: A 68-year-old woman presents as an emergency referral to the Haematology Clinic with extreme lethargy and numbness affecting both feet which has slowly increased over the past few weeks. She has mild asthma for which she takes a low-dose salmeterol/fluticasone inhaler but is otherwise well. Her alcohol consumption is 10 units per week. Her blood pressure is 105/80 mmHg and her heart rate is 95 bpm and regular. She looks pale. Abdominal examination is unremarkable. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 82 g/l 115-155 g/l Mean cell volume (MCV) 105 fl 80-100 fl White cell count (WCC) 4.0×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 113×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 3.7 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 90 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Which of the following is the most likely cause of her blood picture?
explanation: Aplastic Anaemia Media explanations This patient's peripheral neuropathy with macrocytic anaemia, white count at the lower end of the normal range and platelets below the lowerlimit of normal, fits with possible vitamin B12 deficiency. Her age is typical of that seen for the first presentation with pernicious anaemia that is related to a lack of intrinsic factor and impaired vitamin B12 absorption. Both vitamin B12 levels and anti-intrinsic factor antibodies are part of the workup of this patient's anaemia. Intramuscular vitamin B12 injections are the intervention of choice.

stem: A52-year-old pub owner who is known to have alcoholic cirrhosis and portal hypertension is admitted to the Emergency Department with worsening ascites and abdominal pain. An ascitic tap is performed and the total fluid neutrophil count is 310 per mm. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient's ascitic tap appearance?
explanation: E.coliis responsible for 50% or more of cases of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. Abdominal pain and fever are common symptoms, as is the worsening of ascites seen here. Intravenous (IV) piperacillin or tazobactam 4.5g given every 8 hours is a typical intervention. In patients with penicillin allergy,tigecycline IV could be considered as an alternative. It is possible to switch to oral therapy once a definitiveimprovement in clinical signs is seen. Oral therapy may be used from the beginning for patients with mild symptoms.

stem: A 32-year-old woman is referred to the Endocrine Clinic following a recent road traffic accident after which she was found to have bitemporal hemianopia. On further questioning, she also has a lack of libido, vaginal dryness and milk leakage on minimal breast stimulation over the past few months. Her prolactin is 5110 mlU/L(normal value700 mlU/L). Magnetic resonance imaging brain shows a 2 cm pituitary adenoma with optic chiasm compression. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: Although this patient has evidence of optic chiasm compression from her adenoma, approximately 85% of patients with a macroprolactinoma(defined as adenomas measuring 1 cm and over) respond to dopamine agonist therapy with agents such as bromocriptine. Significant improvement in visual fields can be seen in as little as 1-3 days. Changes are visible on imaging after only two weeks. In contrast with microprolactinomas, many patients with larger tumours do eventually require surgery, although shrinkage as a result of dopamine agonist therapy can significantly improve operative outcomes.

stem: A 21-year-old woman presents with carcinoma of the left breast and is found to be BRCA1 positive. Her aunt died of ovarian cancer aged 31 and her sister died of breast cancer aged 27.Her mother is aged 79 years and is currently well. What is the most likely reason that the patient's mother has remained well?
options: new mutation in the patient concerned
Carrier of one copy of the BRCA1 gene
explanation: BRCA1mutations show incomplete penetrance with respect to the development of cancers. At age 70, the mean cumulative cancer risk for breast cancer in BRCA1-positive individuals is 57% and for ovarian cancer,it is 40%. For BRCA2 mutation carriers, the corresponding risks are 49% and 18% respectively. This accounts for the fact that the patient's mother has reached the age of 79 without developing cancer,in contrast to other members of the family.

stem: A 21-year-old man with recently diagnosed type l diabetes is reviewed in the Acute Medical Ward 12 hours after admission with a severe hypoglycaemic episode. He says he thinks it is related to a rugby party where he drank a large amount of alcohol the previous evening. He usually takes a very small amount of insulin. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's hypoglycaemic episode?
explanation: It is thought that alcohol leads to a redistribution of blood flow from the exocrine to the endocrine portions of the pancreas. This leads to increased insulin secretion if the patient has residual beta cell function. This patient takes very small amounts of insulin which suggests he still has considerable endogenous insulin production. In addition, alcohol impairs the counter-regulatory response to hypoglycaemia.

stem: A 76-year-old woman is referred to the Haematology Clinic following two recent episodes of shingles and an abnormal white blood cell count. She admits to feeling tired and off her food over the last three months. Her blood pressure is 122/82 mmHg and her heart rate is 94 bpm and regular and she looks pale. There is marked splenomegaly on palpation of the abdomen. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 101 g/L 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 38.1×10/L 4-11×10/ Lymphocytes 33.2×10/L 1-4×10/ Platelets(PLT) 141×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 140 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 3.0 mmol/l 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 75μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Chronic Lymphocytic Leukaemia Media explanations This patient has impaired immunity to viral infection, splenomegaly and a marked elevation in her lymphocyte count. This is consistent with a diagnosis of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia(CLL). A peripheral blood smear usually reveals the presence of smudge cells. Immunophenotyping confirms the presence of typical B cell antigens including CD5,CD19,CD20 and CD23. Intervention for CLL is contingent upon baseline functional status.

stem: A 28-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus comes to the Antenatal Clinic for review. She is 26 weeks pregnant and is concerned because she has read that her child is at increased risk of neonatal heart block. Which maternal antibody is most likely to cause complete heart block?
explanation: Anti Ro antibodies are associated with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and with Sjgren syndrome. In cases where women with SLE are pregnant and have anti-Ro antibodies, there is a significant risk of neonatal heart block occurring. It has a mortality rate of up to 30% and occurs because of the passage of the anti-Ro antibodies across the placenta. Corticosteroids and intrauterine plasma exchange are possible interventions to reduce the risk of heart block occurring.

stem: A 27-year-old woman who has a new sexual partner presents to the Sexual Health Clinic complaining of dysuria, a mucopurulent vaginal discharge and pain during sexual intercourse. She is tender in the left iliac fossa on abdominal palpation. Nucleic acid amplification test was positive for chlamydia. The urine pregnancy test was negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: Doxycycline 100 mg twice a day for seven days is the intervention of choice for uncomplicated chlamydia infection. Azithromycin is no longer recommended as an alternative first-line option for the treatment of chlamydia because it is less effective than doxycycline in treating rectal chlamydia and co-infection with mycoplasma genitalium is seen which is increasingly resistant to macrolides. Azithromycin can still be considered for use in pregnant women with the infection.

stem: A 27-year-old man presents to the Cancer Genetics Clinic for counselling. His sister has recently been diagnosed with advanced breast cancer. Both his sister and he are positive for the BRCA2 mutation. Which cancer is associated with a particularly increased risk in patients with the BRCA2 mutation?
explanation: The incidence of pancreatic cancer is significantly increased in patients who carry the BRCA2 mutation. There is a standardised incidence ratio of nearly 22, compared to the general population. In men, the risk of prostate cancer is also increased by a BRCA2 carrier status, with a standardised incidence ratio of nearly 5. BRCA1 and BRCA2 are both responsible for DNA repair; hence loss-of-function mutations drive an increased risk as tumour suppression is lost. The BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations are mostly recognised for their role in increasing the risk of breast and ovarian cancers.

stem: A 74-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department by her friend. They were driving together and after one hour, the patient became disorientated and repeatedly questioned where they were driving and why. She became quite distressed and in an attempt to keep her calm, they discussed anecdotes from the past without a problem. At the Emergency Department, she is unable to remember what happened and feels she is back to normal apart from a headache. She has a normal mini-mental state examination score. Physical examination is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The picture here of a transient period of short-term memory loss in the context of continued ability to perform a routine complex task (driving),followed by complete recovery, is consistent with an episode of transient global amnesia. The exact cause is unknown, stress and emotional trauma are both possible causes. Transient global amnesia without other vascular events is associated with a very good prognosis. It is not a risk factor for stroke or ischaemic heart disease and stroke prophylaxis with low-dose aspirin is not required.

stem: A31-year-old woman who is 16 weeks pregnant with her first child presents to the Antenatal Clinic for review. Her blood pressure is noted to be 149/92 mmHg and has been elevated on the past three visits to the clinic. Her pre-pregnancy blood pressure was normal. Her body mass index is 27 kg/m.Serum creatinine level and urine examination are both normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step for her blood pressure?
explanation: This patient has gestational hypertension but there are no signs or symptoms of pre-eclampsia.The blood pressure is at a level that requires intervention and labetalol is thefirst choice therapy according to NICE guidelines.100 mg twice a day is the initial recommended starting dose, it can be titrated up to 800 mg total daily dose. Alternatives to labetalol according to NICE guidelines include methyldopa and nifedipine.

stem: A 42-year-old woman presents to the Dermatology Clinic with a constantly flushed face, reddening around the nose and prominent sebaceous glands. Examination reveals erythematous cheeks with prominent telangiectasias and large inflamed sebaceous glands around the nose. The skin is dry. The condition began 12-18 months ago with intermittent facial flushing which gradually became more prominent. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial intervention?
explanation: Topical metronidazole 0.75% is the most commonly used option for the initial treatment of rosacea, the likely diagnosis here, given the skin flushing that has become constant erythema, prominent sebaceous glands and dry skin. Azelaic acid 15% can be used as an alternative in patients who have rosacea with particularly marked inflammation.

stem: A 61-year-old woman who has metastatic breast cancer presents to the Palliative Care Clinic complaining of worsening pain affecting her left humerus and right femur. Current pain relief includes paracetamol 4 g per day and codeine phosphate 240 mg per day. Which of the following is the most appropriate conversion dose when switching codeine to oral morphine?
explanation: The conversion factor for moving oral codeine phosphate doses to oral morphine is 0.1.This means that 240 mg of codeine phosphate translates to an oral morphine dose of 24 mg per day. Initially, this should be given as short-acting morphine, with the possibility of breakthrough dosing to control the patient's bony pain. Once a stable dose is achieved, this can be converted to morphine slow-release tablets. Difficuty:Average External Links Pain relief - palliative care Dose Equivalents and Changing Opi..

stem: A 27-year-old man from Egypt is referred to the Rheumatology Clinic with recurrent oral and genital ulceration, erythema nodosum and anterior uveitis. Which of the following is the most likely human leukocyte antigen type of this patient?
explanation: This patient's symptoms with oral and genital ulceration, erythema nodosum and anterior uveitis fit with a diagnosis of Behcet's disease, which is more common in patients of Mediterranean /African descent.

stem: A 20-year-old man is treated in the Emergency Department. He was admitted with stridor, an urticarial rash, hypotension and tachycardia, which responded to treatment with intramuscular adrenaline and fluid resuscitation. Which of the following is the most useful investigation to confirm the underlying diagnosis?
explanation: Mast cell tryptase, which is a mast cell-specific protease,increases following mast cell degranulation. The level peaks after the first hour and remains elevated for a period of around six hours. It can be used to help confirm a diagnosis of anaphylaxis when this is in doubt. Not every case of anaphylaxis leads to a rise in tryptase, the sensitivity and specificity of the test is around 95%.

stem: A31-year-old woman who is 20 weeks pregnant presents to the Emergency Department complaining of left-sided pleuritic chest pain that is worse on inspiration. She has no cough and no history of fever. Her blood pressure is 105/80mmHg, her heart rate is 95 bpm and regular. Chest is clear on auscultation. Oxygen saturation is 92% on air. She has an abdomen consistent with a 20-week pregnancy. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 112 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count 5.1×10/ 4-11×10/L Platelets 207×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium (Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 3.7 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmoll/L Creatinine 75 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Chest X-ray Normal Half dose VQ left sided perfusion defect consistent with a pulmonary scan embolism Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation: Low molecular weight heparin is the treatment of choice for pulmonary embolism in pregnancy. A dose of 1 mg/kg of subcutaneous enoxaparin every 12 hours is recommended. Although subcutaneous injection is a burden for women with pulmonary embolism the benefits of low molecular weight heparin are clear. Treatment is usually continued for the remainder of the pregnancy and for at least six weeks postnatally.

stem: A 59-year-old man visits the Diabetes Clinic for review. His type Il diabetes is usually managed with metformin only, although he has recently been admitted to the hospital with an episode of heart failure. A decision is made to start him on dapagliflozin. What is the mode of action of dapagliflozin?
explanation: Dapagliflozin is a sodium-glucose transport protein 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor.This means that it blocks sodium and glucose reabsorption in the kidney so that both are excreted. The class of SGLT2 inhibitors not only reduces blood glucose levels, but also has positive effects on renal and heart failure outcomes. Their diuretic effect is short-lived. It is thought that they improve mitochondrial function and make the patient resistant to oxidative stress. The class is associated with an increased risk of genital infection, particularly in women, although this is seen most often in the first few weeks of therapy.

stem: A76-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Assessment Unit with severe abdominal pain which started six hours ago. She had an episode of bloody diarrhoea the previous day. She has atrial fibrillation and type Il diabetes for which she takes metformin and dapagliflozin. Her blood pressure is 90/50 mmHg and her heart rate is 110 bpm(atrial fibrillation). There are signs of peritonism with quiet bowel sounds on examination of the abdomen. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 112 g/l 115-155 g/L White cell count(WCC) 15.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 210×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 5.2 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 195μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Glycated haemoglobin 67 mmol/mol 52 mmol/mol Lactate 4.1 mmol/L 0.5-2.2 mmol/L Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This patient has evidence of vascular disease with diabetes mellitus and atrial fibrillation. The episode of bloody diarrhoea coupled with now continuous abdominal pain and an elevated lactate level is suggestive of ischaemic colitis. Computed tomography angiography is the initial investigation of choice and could potentially demonstrate mesenteric artery occlusion due to emboli or thrombus. Early diagnosis is crucial, coupled with an assessment of the likely operative risk to decide whether laparotomy and resection of any area of the ischaemic bowel would be appropriate.

stem: A 68-year-old man presents to the Ophthalmology Clinic complaining that his near vision has deteriorated over the past few months, particularly with respect to the left eye. He also says that the sizes of objects look different between his two eyes. He is having particular problems with seeing at night when he sees a dark patch in his left field of vision, which takes some time to clear. Fundoscopy reveals bilateral optic nerve drusen, more marked in the left eye. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The appearance of this patient's retina is consistent with age-related macular degeneration, with drusen more marked on the side with the worst vision (the left). Deterioration in near vision is noted first and impaired night vision and impaired dark adaptation are also typical of the condition. Fluorescein angiography is used to assess for neovascularisation and exudates, which point towards a diagnosis of active wet macular degeneration, which is likely to benefit from treatment with an anti-vascular endothelial growth factor biological agent.

stem: A 23-year-old woman who has cystic fibrosis is reviewed in the Respiratory Clinic. She has had four chest infections in the past year, limited exercise tolerance, uses home oxygen and is colonised with pseudomonas. She has previously been non-compliant with antibiotic therapy on two occasions. Her body mass index is 15 kg/m(2). Her fasting glucose is 6.4 mmol/L. What is the most important contraindication to a lung transplant?
options: Non-compliance with medication on two occasions
explanation: Malnutrition is a contraindication to lung transplant because it is associated with increased perioperative complications and delayed healing. Obesity is also a contraindication to lung transplant, although this is not really seen in patients with cystic fibrosis. This patient needs intensive dietitian input to improve her nutritional status before moving to transplant. She may develop diabetes because of her increased calorie intake, but this can be managed with insulin therapy.

stem: An 18-year-old woman is diagnosed with systemic lupus erythematosus. She is thought to have an inherited complement deficiency. Which complement factor is most likely to be deficient in this patient?
explanation: Deficiencies of the early components of the complement pathway including C1q,C1r/s, C2 and C4 can lead to the development of premature autoimmune disease including systemic lupus erythematosus. This may be due to reduced clearance of apoptotic cells and increased development of autoantigens. C2 deficiency is also associated with the development of premature cardiovascular disease and recurrent bacterial infections.

stem: A52-year-old woman is referred to the Endocrine Clinic with worsening tiredness and weight gain over the past six months. She also feels short of breath, particularly when she lies flat at night. Her blood pressure is 155/90 mmHg, her heart rate is 65 bpm and regular. She has a smooth goitre. Her body mass index is 31 kg/m. nvestigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 132 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 7.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 181×10/L 150-400×10/ Sodium(Na+) 134 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.9 mmol/l 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 75μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Thyroid-stimulating hormone(TSH) 11.2 mU/L 0.3-4.2 mU/L Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Hypothyroidism Media explanations Flashcards This patient has a smooth goitre with symptoms of hypothyroidism and a marked elevation in TSH. This clinical picture fits with a diagnosis of Hashimoto's thyroiditis. Typically, there is autoimmune destruction of thyroxine-producing cells and TSH receptor-blocking antibodies. Treatment is with thyroxine replacement. Better recognition of the condition means that myxoedema coma as a presentation of severe hypothyroidism is now rarely seen.

stem: A 62-year-old man returns to the Infectious Disease Clinic four weeks after starting quadruple therapy for pulmonary tuberculosis. His General Practitioner is concerned about abnormal liver function tests. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 136 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 6.7×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 181×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 95μmol/L 50-120 μmol/l Alanine aminotransferase(ALT) 84 U/L 1-40 U/L Alkaline phosphatase 179 IU/L 30-130 IU/L Bilirubin 21μmol/L 21μmol/L Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: Drug-induced Liver Injury explanations In this situation, with a minor rise in both alanine aminotransferase and alkaline phosphatase levels and normal bilirubin level, anti-tuberculous therapy may be safely continued. If the alanine aminotransferase level is more than five times the upper limit of normal, or there is any elevation of bilirubin or the patient develops symptomatic hepatitis then all treatment should be stopped temporarily.

stem: A 21-year-old man is reviewed in the Cardiology Clinic, having suffered a cardiac arrest while swimming. He was in ventricular tachycardia at the local pool and received one shock to achieve sinus rhythm. His father died of cardiac arrest at the age of 34 years. His QT interval is prolonged on 12 lead ECG. What cardiac ion channel is most likely to be abnormal on the ECG?
explanation: Long QT1 is the most common form of congenital long QT syndrome, the most likely cause of this patient's cardiac arrest. It occurs because of an abnormality in the lks alpha subunit of the cardiac potassium channel. Significant rhythm disturbance is seen in association with periods of exercise and periods of emotion. Low- risk patients who have not suffered significant arrhythmias can be managed with beta-blockade. In patients who are high-risk,(like this one), an implantable cardioverter defibrillator should be considered.

stem: A49-year-old woman presents to the General Practitioner complaining of having to rush to pass urine and occasionally not making it in time. She has increased urinary frequency and usually has abdominal discomfort before she needs to pass urine. Reducing her consumption of tea and coffee has not improved her symptoms. Physical examination is normal and her body mass index is 24 kg/m. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 132 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 7.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 189×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 75μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Urine Negative Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: Urinary incontinence (Female) explanations This patient's symptoms fit well with urge incontinence which is related to overactive bladder syndrome. In this case, lifestyle measures, such as reducing tea and coffee and bladder training, are the first step. If these are ineffective, then anti-cholinergic therapy is indicated with an agent such as oxybutynin. In the event this is not tolerated, longer-acting anticholinergics such as tolterodine may be appropriate, or switching to a beta-3 agonist is an alternative. Where the body mass index is greater than 30 kg/m,weight reduction may improve symptoms.

stem: A71-year-old man presents to the Neurology Clinic complaining of severe dizziness and vertigo. This came on all of a sudden one morning when he sat up in bed. The feeling of dizziness is worse when he turns his head to the left at about 45 degrees and lies back. It begins a few seconds after he reaches a supine position. Neurological examination is normal, apart from the Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre which reproduces the dizziness. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: This patient has benign paroxysmal positional vertigo with a positive Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre. The most appropriate intervention is an attempt at canalith repositioning with the Epley manoeuvre. This involves the use of a mastoid bone oscillator to promote canalith movement, moving the head through all relevant positions to ensure repositioning.

stem: A72-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department having suffered a seizure at home. According to her husband she had generalised limb jerking which lasted for around two minutes, she also bit her tongue and was incontinent of urine. She had a small stroke one year earlier, for which she now takes clopidogrel 75 mg and has hypertension. Neurological examination in the Emergency Department is unremarkable. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 132 g/L 115-155 g/L White cell count(WCC) 6.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 280×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.7 mmol/l 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 75μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Glucose 7.2 mmol/L 3.9-7.0 mmol/L Which of the following is the most likely cause of her seizure?
explanation: Epilepsy and Seizures Media explanations Cerebrovascular disease is the most common cause of epilepsy in the elderly. It also fits with this patient having suffered a small stroke in the previous year. Compromised vascular supply often related to small vessel disease can result in neuronal irritability, which increases the risk of seizures. A number of options exist as monotherapy to reduce the risk of further seizures including lamotrigine, levetiracetam and lacosamide.

stem: A 35-year-old man presents to the Rheumatology Clinic complaining of pins and needles over the fourth and fifth fingers of his right hand and weakness of the muscles of the hypothenar eminence. He is a builder and regularly uses tools such as a sledge hammer for his work. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Repeated use of heavy tools including a sledgehammer or large power drill can lead to pressure and swelling over the cubital tunnel, also known as Guyon's canal. This leads to symptoms associated with compression of the ulnar nerve, including weakness of the muscles of the hypothenar eminence and sensory loss over the fourth and fifth fingers. First-line treatment is with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and splinting.

stem: A 24-year-old man is reviewed in the Oncology Clinic following surgery and chemotherapy for a left testicular teratoma. What is the most useful marker to monitor for tumour recurrence?
explanation: Alpha-fetoprotein is elevated in testicular teratomas and can be used as a tumour marker to monitor for the recurrence of the disease. It has a long half-Life of 5-7 days and can therefore be measured in the clinic. Alpha-fetoprotein levels are also elevated in patients with advanced liver cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. Lactate dehydrogenase levels are also elevated in testicular carcinoma, although it is a non- specific marker versus alpha-fetoprotein.

stem: An 18-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with his brother. He has had increasing shortness of breath and decreased exercise tolerance over the past six months. He has intermittently attended health services over his life and has no hospital records. His blood pressure is 155/90mmHg in the right arm and 122/78 mmHg in the left arm. He has a pansystolic murmur heard loudest in the left infraclavicular area and under the left scapula. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
explanation: This patient's symptoms are consistent with a late presentation of coarctation of the aorta, with progressive cardiac failure and differential blood pressures between the arms and a systolic murmur loudest in the left infraclavicular area. ChestX-ray may demonstrate signs of left ventricular failure, the indentation of the aortic shadow, or rib notching due to pressure from collateral blood vessels. Echocardiogram cardiography can be used to demonstrate the gradient across the coarctation. Surgical correction is the intervention of choice.

stem: A 29-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department in a drowsy and agitated state having taken 56×75mg amitryptiline, an unknown quantity of diazepam and wine. Her Glasgow Coma Scale score is 11,blood pressure is 90/50 mmHg and her heart rate is 97 bpm and regular. Investigations: Investigations Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 102 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 8.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 75×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 133 mmol/l 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 5.1 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Bicarbonate 16 mmol/L 22-30 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 132μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Electrocardiogram Sinus rhythm, QRS 120ms
explanation: The QRS prolongation in patients with a tricyclic antidepressant overdose is associated with a poor prognosis both from the risk of ventricular tachycardia and also the risk of seizures. When QRS prolongation is greater than 100 ms then intravenous (IV) sodium bicarbonate should be given.1-2mmol/kg should be given as a rapidIV push,usually with 8.4% bicarbonate solution. It can be repeated after 5 minutes in the event there is no response.

stem: A74-year-old man presents to the Rheumatology Clinic complaining of pain and stiffness affecting his left hip. He is now unable to walk to the local supermarket without pain and this is not helped by regular paracetamol. He has pain and limitation of movement on hip flexion and lateral rotation. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Calcium 2.3 mmol/L 2.1-2.65 mmol/L Alkaline phosphatase 92 U/L 30-130 U/l C-reactive protein 8 mg/l 10 mg/l X-ray left hip Joint space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis, osteophytes Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This patient's X-ray changes are typical of osteoarthritis with joint space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis, and osteophyte formation. The normal blood results for calcium and alkaline phosphatase also support this as the underlying diagnosis. Given that regular paracetamol is unhelpful in controlling his pain a non- steroidal anti-inflammatory drug may be appropriate, although a hip replacement is likely to be required.

stem: A 74-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with dull abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea over the past 12 hours. She is hypotensive and blood tests reveal an elevated lactate. She has a history of hypertension, type Il diabetes and atrial fibrillation. Which area of the colon is most likely to be affected?
explanation: The most likely diagnosis in an elderly patient with vascular risk factors and atrial fibrillation presenting with abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea is ischaemic colitis. There are two watershed areas with respect to the arterial supply to the colon. One is the splenic flexure and the other is the rectosigmoid junction. At the splenic flexure, the superior mesenteric artery which supplies the colon from the caecum to the splenic flexure anastomoses with the inferior mesenteric artery which supplies the area from the flexure to the rectum. At the rectosigmoid junction the inferior mesenteric artery anastomoses with a branch of the superior rectal artery. These watershed areas can be susceptible to low blood flow,and hence to ischaemic colitis.

stem: A 39-year-old woman returns to the Psychiatry Clinic three months after beginning cognitive behavioural therapy for depressive symptoms after the break-up of her relationship. Her symptoms have worsened; she is now waking at 04:30 each morning, has lost 5 kg in weight and is suffering increasing thoughts of hopelessness. Physical examination is unremarkable and her body mass index is 20.5 kg/m. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: In a patient with worsening depressive symptoms despite cognitive behavioural therapy, a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor is the most appropriate next step. They are effective and well tolerated, compared to other potential options such as tricyclic antidepressants which have anticholinergic side-effects and are much more dangerous in overdose. Other agents such as serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors may also have a role.

stem: A 39-year-old man of Chinese descent presents to the Emergency Department with a generalised erythematous rash with numerous vesicles and necrotic ulcers. He also has conjunctivitis and extensive mucosal ulceration. He has a fever, is short of breath and has a dry cough. His temperature is 38.1°℃, his blood pressure is 100/70 mmHg and his heart rate is 95 bpm and regular. He takes a number of medications for hypertension, pain relief and epilepsy. Which medication is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
explanation: This patient has evidence of Stevens-Johnson syndrome with generalised erythema, blisters,ulcers, conjunctivitis and fever.Given he is of Chinese descent, the possibility of Stevens-Johnson syndrome related to carbamazepine use should be considered. This is related to the presence of the human leukocyte antigen- B*1502, which is seen in around 10% of Chinese patients. If carbamazepine is to be used in Chinese patients, then human leukocyte antigen testing is recommended. Withdrawal of carbamazepine as soon as possible is advised.

stem: A52-year-old man presents to the Gastroenterology Clinic for a review after a repeat endoscopy six months after his first one which confirmed Barrett's oesophagus with low-grade dysplasia. After six months of treatment with a high-dose proton pump inhibitor, the biopsies still show low-grade dysplasia. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Continue high dose proton pump inhibitor
explanation: Radiofrequency ablation is the preferred treatment intervention for Barrett's oesophagus. Over a three-year period, 26.5% of patients progress to high-grade dysplasia or cancer without ablation. This is vastly reduced when patients are treated with ablation. There is more evidence to support the use of radiofrequency ablation versus other measures such as cryotherapy.

stem: A 36-year-old woman presents to the Rheumatology Clinic complaining of pain and joint swelling affecting her fingers and toes and both wrists and ankles over the past three months. She has been taking regular ibuprofen although it has had no significant impact on her symptoms. There is pain and stiffness over several metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 135 g/l 115-155 g/L White cell count 7.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 341×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 3.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 105μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L C-reactive protein 65 mg/L 10 mg/L Rheumatoid factor Negative Hand X-ray Soft tissue swelling and periarticular osteopaenia Which of the following is the most useful next investigation?
explanation: Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (CCP) antibodies are a recommended next investigation in patients with suspected rheumatoid arthritis, as evidenced by the synovitis in a classical distribution, where rheumatoid factor testing has proved negative. Anti-CCP antibodies are more specific than rheumatoid factor in making a diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis and are more sensitive in predicting aggressive erosive disease. Anti-CCP antibody positivity can be used as a trigger for therapy intensification.

stem: A 27-year-old man, who is human immunodeficiency virus(HIV) positive, has recently started quadruple therapy with antituberculous medication including ethambutol, rifampicin, isoniazid and pyrazinamide. He complains of symptoms of peripheral neuropathy with pins and needles affecting his hands and feet. Which drug is the most likely cause of this patient's neuropathy?
explanation: Peripheral neuropathy is a well-known consequence of isoniazid therapy, the risk of which is increased in patients who are HIV-positive and those with alcoholism. Supplementation with low-dose pyridoxine is recommended to reduce the risk of neuropathy occurring. At high doses, it can be used to treat isoniazid- related neuropathy.

stem: A54-year-old man presents to the Dermatology Clinic with an itchy rash affecting the flexor surfaces of both wrists and raised white-coloured, streaky lesions in the mouth. Examination reveals small, white- topped, raised, violaceous lesions affecting both wrists, each 2-5 mm in diameter. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The lesions described here are typical of those seen in lichen planus.The white areas which top the papules are known as Wickham's striae. The exact cause of lichen planus is not known, although it is thought to be a T cell mediated autoimmune disease. Treatment is not always needed, with most lesions clearing within a year. Topical steroids are the initial intervention of choice. In cases where there is an inadequate response, then azathioprine, calcineurin inhibitors and mycophenolate mofetil are all potential systemic interventions.

stem: A 32-year-old man, who is human immunodeficiency virus(HIV)-positive, presents to the Infectious Diseases Clinic with progressively worsening nodular skin lesions which have developed over the past six months. He has a number of nodular red-brown skin lesions, which affect both the skin and mucous membranes. Which human herpes virus is the most likely cause of this patient's skin lesions?
explanation: This patient has skin lesions consistent with Kaposi's sarcoma, which is prevalent in patients with HIV who have a high viral load and a depressed CD4 count. It is caused by human herpes virus 8,also known as Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpes virus. The mainstay of therapy for Kaposi's sarcoma is highly active anti- retroviral therapy to reduce viral load and improve immune recognition of human herpes virus 8.Individual lesions can also be treated locally, including with cryotherapy and electrodesiccation with curettage.

stem: An 18-year-old presents to the Emergency Department 72 hours after being prescribed amoxicillin for pharyngitis. She is worried that her symptoms are getting worse. She has a maculopapular skin rash and has suffered more fevers over the past 24 hours. Her blood pressure is 141/84 mmHg and her heart rate is 88 bpm and regular. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 123 g/l 115-155 g/L White cell count (WCC) 8.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Eosinophils 3.1×109/L 0.05-0.5×10/L Platelets 291×109/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/l 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 5.2 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 182μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Urine Blood 1+, protein 1+ Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Interstitial Nephritis explanations Acute interstitial nephritis presents between 2 and 60 days after exposure to beta-lactam antibiotics and is associated with fever, a maculopapular rash, eosinophilia and haematuria. Abnormal liver function tests are also seen. Other antibiotics, including quinolones, macrolides and cephalosporins may also cause nephritis. Where non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents are the cause,the onset is usually more gradual. Withdrawal of the causative agent is the most important intervention.

stem: A 23-year-old man presents to the Gastroenterology Clinic for a follow-up appointment after an admission six weeks earlier where he had the first presentation of ulcerative colitis. He has now reduced his corticosteroid dose to 10 mg of prednisolone per day. A colonoscopy has shown the disease is confined to the rectum and the left side of the colon. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial therapy for long-term ulcerative colitis prophylaxis?
explanation: For the maintenance of remission in ulcerative colitis, a dose of 400-800 mg three times a day of mesalazine is the preferred treatment option. Mesalazine is a 5-amino salicylic acid compound that acts locally at the level of the colonic mucosa to reduce inflammation. In patients who experience a flare-up on mesalazine corticosteroids can be reintroduced. Azathioprine can be used as a steroid-sparing agent if required.

stem: A 29-year-old woman is reviewed 30 minutes after admission to the Emergency Department with an acute exacerbation of asthma. She has received continuous salbutamol nebulisers since admission to the unit. For the previous five days at home, she has doubled her inhaled fluticasone/salmeterol inhaler and has been taking 40 mg of oral prednisolone. Her blood pressure is 122/82 mmHg, her heart rate is 105 bpm and regular. She has bilateral wheeze on auscultation of the chest. Peak flow is 220 U/min(450 predicted). Her oxygen saturation is 96% on 10 litres of oxygen per minute. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: Intravenous magnesium is recommended as the treatment option in patients with acute severe asthma who have not gained control of symptoms on standard interventions, including back-to-back nebulisers. Magnesium is given at a dose of 1.2-2g over a period of 20 minutes.

stem: A21-year-old man presents to the Gastroenterology Clinic complaining of abdominal pain and intermittent constipation. He has already had two colonoscopies which have been reported as normal and a range of normal blood tests, but he is convinced that he has colon cancer. His grandfather recently died of colon cancer aged 71 years. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: This patient has illness anxiety disorder, the trigger of which is likely to have been the death of his grandfather from colon cancer. He has already had the gold standard investigation repeated twice, so there is no indication for further testing. Cognitive behavioural therapy is the gold standard intervention to address fears and beliefs around colon cancer and institute strategies for re-education, as well as to improve resilience with respect to worries and stressors. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor therapy may be offered,in addition, for patients with prominent depressive symptoms.

stem: A 22-year-old man who has familial hypercholesterolaemia presents to the Endocrinology Clinic for review. He wishes to start evinacumab. What is the mode of action of evinacumab?
explanation: Evinacumab inhibits angiopoietin-like protein-3(ANGPTL3) and is a monoclonal antibody indicated for the treatment of hypercholesterolaemia in patients with familial hypercholesterolaemia.In patients treated with standard-of-care therapy, the drug lowers cholesterol by 47% over a six-month period.Angiopoietin-like protein-3(ANGPTL3) acts as a dual inhibitor of endothelial lipase and lipoprotein lipase. In humans who carry one copy of the loss of function polymorphism for ANGPTL3, low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol is reduced. In those who carry two mutations, low LDL, high-density lipoprotein(HDL) and triglycerides are seen.

stem: A 29-year-old man presents to the Sexually Transmitted Disease Clinic with a painful ulcer affecting his glans penis. He has just returned from a business trip to West Africa. Examination reveals a 1 cm ulcer affecting the glans penis and inguinal lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient's symptoms?
explanation: Chancroid is rarely seen in the UK but is endemic in parts of Africa and the Caribbean. It is of concern to the World Health Organisation because, as an ulcerative sexually transmitted disease, it may increase the risk of HIV transmission. It typically presents with one or two painful ulcers 1-2 cm across and painful inguinal lymphadenopathy. Azithromycin given orally and ceftriaxone given intramuscularly can both be used as a single-dose intervention for the treatment of chancroid.

stem: A29-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department by her colleagues after displaying very strange behaviour at work. She booked a number of meetings but walked out part-way through and has not finished any of her projects in the past few months. She speaks extremely fast and flits from one idea to another. She recently fired the translation services at her office because she told them she speaks 12 languages. She suffered a bout of depression five years earlier. What is the most appropriate long-term treatment for this patient's psychological presentation?
explanation: Risperidone is a dopamine antagonist antipsychotic and can be very useful in the initial treatment of mania. It can manage both symptoms of agitation and hyperactivity and delusions. In this case, theinability to finish tasks, out-of-character behaviour,inappropriate affect, pressure of speech and claims around speaking 12 languages all fit with mania as the cause of the patient's symptoms. Later on,in the course of the disease,a mood stabiliser should be introduced. Potential options include lithium and sodium valproate, although given this woman's age, contraceptive advice is crucial.

stem: An 18-year-old woman is referred to the Renal Clinic with persistent lethargy and muscle cramps. She has lost consciousness on at least two occasions in the pharmacy where she works. She is on the 25th centile for height and has a body mass index of 22 kg/m. Her blood pressure is 100/70 mmHg. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 122 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count(WCC) 6.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 301×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 143 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 3.0 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Bicarbonate 35 mmol/L 22-32 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 85μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Magnesium 0.84 mmol/L 0.7-1.05 mmol/L Urinary calcium excretion 9 mmol/24 hours 2.5-7.5 mmol/24 hours Which of the following is the most likely site of this patient's kidney defect?
options: Thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle
explanation: Bartter syndrome characteristically involves a mutation that leads to defective functioning of the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle. This leads to a hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis and increased urinary calcium excretion.

stem: A 62-year-old man is reviewed in the Oncology Clinic three years after the initial resection of Dukes B colon cancer. He has felt increasingly tired, with vague right upper quadrant pain over the past few months. An ultrasound scan of the liver has shown multiple circular abnormalities suspicious of hepatic metastases. Which tumour marker is likely to be most useful to measure in this case?
explanation: Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) describes a series of glycoproteins that are involved in cell adhesion. They are thought to be critical to the metastatic dissemination of colon cancer cells. Elevated levels of CEA are seen in colon cancer, cervical cancer, lung cancer, ovarian cancer and breast cancer, as well as in some urinary tract tumours. It can be used to monitor for colon cancer recurrence.

stem: A65-year-old woman who has end stage renal failure presents to the Renal Clinic complaining of severe bone pains and lethargy. Her blood pressure is 155/82 mmHg, her heart rate is 82 and regular. Her body mass index is 23 kg/m. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 97 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count(WCC) 6.8×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 199×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Phosphate 1.8 mmol/L 0.7-1.5 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 297 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Calcium 2.85 mmol/L 2.1-2.65 mmol/L Alkaline phosphatase 239 IU/L 30-130 IU/L Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This patient has end-stage renal failure with elevated calcium, phosphate and alkaline phosphatase levels, as well as symptoms,including lethargy and bony pain. This fits with a diagnosis of tertiary hyperparathyroidism. Although we are not provided with the parathyroid hormone level,it is likely to be significantly elevated. Operative assessment for possible parathyroidectomy is the most appropriate next step, with surgery being the most appropriate intervention. In the event that the patient is unfit for surgery, then long-term therapy with cinacalcet may be an option.

stem: A 39-year-old sheep farmer is referred to the Infectious Disease Clinic after complaining of vague right upper quadrant pain and intermittent fevers over the last few months. He has tenderness in the right upper quadrant on abdominal palpation and you can feel a 3 cm liver edge. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 112 g/l 135-175 g/L White cell count(WCC) 7.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 161×10/L 150-400×10/L C-reactive protein(CRP) 85 mg/l 10 mg/L Sodium(Na+) 141 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 3.7 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 85μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Alanine aminotransferase(ALT) 122 U/L 1-40 U/L Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) 391 U/L 30-130 U/L Abdominal ultrasound 5×10 cm simple liver cyst Which of the following is the most appropriate initial intervention?
explanation: This man is a sheep farmer who presents with fevers, an enlarged liver and a simple cyst. This raises the possibility of active Echinococcus infection leading to hydatid disease of the liver. ALbendazole is the initial intervention of choice with mebendazole a potential alternative. Three potential options are usually considered for the treatment of hydatid disease: · the puncture, aspiration, injection, and respiration technique. This involves percutaneous puncture of the cyst, aspiration of cyst fluid,injection of chemicals and re-puncture · surgical removal of the cyst · long term anti-infective drug treatment with albendazole.

stem: A32-year-old woman complains of excessive daytime sleepiness in the Sleep Medicine Clinic. She has had one episode of collapse while laughing in the past few months where she appeared to lose all muscle tone. She often feels something touching her skin as she falls asleep. Her husband reports that she seems to sit up in bed with her eyes open on occasions when she is deeply asleep. Physical examination is unremarkable, apart from her body mass index which is 31 kg/m. What is the most likely cause of this patient's daytime sleepiness?
explanation: This patient has excessive daytime sleepiness, hypnogogic hallucinations and automatism. She has also had at least one episode of cataplexy characterised by sudden collapse, with muscular weakness. Although her body mass index is 31kg/m,there are no reported symptoms of sleep apnoea such as stopping breathing or excessive snoring. Good sleep hygiene is important in managing narcolepsy. The stimulant modafinil is the mainstay treatment for daytime sleepiness.

stem: The local university has an outbreak of meningococcal meningitis. One of the students is concerned about catching the infection. What is the most common mode of transmission of meningococcus?
explanation: Infection is transmitted by droplets or secretions from the upper respiratory tract. The most likely source of infection of symptomatic strains appears to be household members or close friends who are asymptomatic carriers. Meningococci may spread from the nasopharynx to adjacent areas, sometimes leading to pneumonia or sinusitis. Asymptomatic nasopharyngeal carriage is transient and eventually resolves after days to months, leaving protective immunity against the organism.

stem: A71-year-old man presents with sudden-onset right-sided spastic hemiparesis accompanied by right-sided fine touch, vibration and proprioception loss. He also has paralysis of the left lateral rectus muscle. What is the most likely site of this patient's brain lesion?
explanation: Medial pontine syndrome occurs due to occlusion of the paramedian branches of the basilar artery. It leads to the disruption of the corticospinal tract, which leads to contralateral spastic hemiparesis and disruption of the medial lemniscus. This results in loss of fine touch, vibration and position sense on the contralateral side and abducens nerve palsy on the ipsilateral side that leads to lateral rectus muscle weakness.

stem: A42-year-old man has a lumbar puncture some 15 hours after presenting with sudden-onset, severe occipital headache and neck stiffness. Cerebrospinal testing is undertaken. What finding on cerebrospinal analysis is most suggestive of subarachnoid haemorrhage?
explanation: Bilirubin is the by-product of haem breakdown, which is produced by the action of the haem oxygenase enzyme. It is responsible for the change in colour of the cerebrospinal fluid to yellow(xanthochromia). The presence of xanthochromia some 15 hours after symptoms of headache is consistent with possible subarachnoid haemorrhage. It may also be seen in severe systemicjaundice.

stem: A71-year-old man is referred to the Haematology Clinic after presenting to his General Practitioner with lethargy and elevated haemoglobin. He also complains about increased itching over the past few months. Apart from hypertension he has no other past medical history. His blood pressure is 145/88mmHg and his heart rate is 72 bpm. Abdominal examination reveals moderate splenomegaly. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 185 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 9.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 395×10/L 150-400×109/L Erythropoietin 2.0 IU/L 2.5-18.5 IU/L Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This patient has an isolated increase in haemoglobin level and a reduction in erythropoietin level. This is coupled with splenomegaly, which fits with a diagnosis of primary polycythaemia. Testing for the JAK2 V617F mutation may also be helpful because it is positive in more than 90% of patients with primary polycythaemia. Phlebotomy and low-dose aspirin are the mainstays of initial therapy to reduce cardiovascular risk. Higher-risk patients also receive cytoreductive therapy. Polycythaemia Vera Media explanations.

stem: An 18-year-old man presents to the Endocrine Clinic complaining of difficulty forming relationships and a lack of sex drive. He has no sense of smell but is otherwise well. He is of normal height, his body mass index is 23 kg/m.He has an absence of facial and axillary hair and sparse pubic hair. His penis and testes are small. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Kallmann syndrome is caused by a failure of the olfactory bulb to develop. This means that gonadotrophin- releasing hormone (GnRH) is not properly secreted. There is a subsequent failure to produce luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone. Patients with Kallmann syndrome do not, therefore, enter puberty properly. On direct questioning, they often report an impaired sense of smell. Treatment is with testosterone if fertility is not required, or with pulsed GnRH in patients where there is a wish to establish fertility. Q. Answered Flagged Delayed Puberty or Short Stature explanations.

stem: A 19-year-old man is referred to the Rheumatology Clinic. He has had several months of lower back pain and stiffness which lasts for around two hours each morning and it is currently preventing him from working. He has also had a previous episode of plantar fasciitis affecting his left foot which has required a corticosteroid injection. Examination reveals a limitation of forward and lateral flexion of the lumbar spine. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 137 g/l 135-175 g/L White cell count 7.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 385×10/L 150-400×10/L C-reactive protein 55 mg/L 10 mg/L Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This patient's presentation with inflammatory back pain that is worse in the morning with limitation of forward and lateral flexion of the lumbar spine, coupled with plantar fasciitis and a raised C-reactive protein fits well with a diagnosis of ankylosing spondylitis. Magnetic resonanceimaging scanning can be useful to diagnose early sacroiliitis and is more sensitive than a plain X-ray. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and physiotherapy are the initial therapy of choice. Tumour necrosis factor-alpha inhibitors should be considered early in patients who fail to respond to NSAIDs. Ankylosing Spondylitis Media explanations.

stem: A42-year-old woman presents to the General Practitioner with abdominal bloating, intermittent diarrhoea and increased production of bowel gas over the past few months. She already takes omeprazole for gastro- oesophageal reflux disease and has systemic sclerosis. Her abdomen is soft but there is mild distension and minor tenderness on palpation. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 101 g/l 115-155 g/L White cell count (WCC) 8.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets (PLT) 191×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 141 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 3.7 mmol/l 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine(Cr) 123 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Which of the following is the most useful investigation?
explanation: This patient's symptoms are consistent with small bowel bacterial overgrowth, which is strongly associated with systemic sclerosis because of disordered motility. A number of methods are used to confirm the diagnosis. These include jejunal aspiration and culture, which is not preferred because it requires an endoscopy,and a range of breath tests. Breath tests include 14-C D-xylose, hydrogen breath testing using glucose or lactulose and 14-C-glycocholic acid. A range of antibiotics have shown efficacy in treating small bowel bacterial overgrowth including metronidazole, tetracyclines and rifaximin. Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) Media explanations.
